Ken Kutaragi: I wanted Microsoft to make the Xbox, and I love Nintendo
The father of PlayStation speaks to The Game Business
Christopher Dring and James Batchelor
Nov 24
Listen now on Apple , Spotify or YouTube
In This Edition,
Ken Kutaragi on…
The launch of PS1, PS2 and PS3
The future of consoles
The impact of AI
Plus, Nintendo, Xbox, Sega and more
In October, video game legend Ken Kutaragi - the father of PlayStation himself - visited the UK to talk with us on-stage at the Game Republic New Horizons conference
In a wide ranging interview that touched upon the past and future of the video game industry, Kutaragi reflected on some of the key moments that not only shaped PlayStation, but the industry as a whole. He also discussed his views on the future of the business, and whether game consoles are part of it.
He conducted the full interview in English, and as a Japanese man, it can be tricky to follow. As a result, we’ve decided against an audio-only/podcast version of this edition. Instead, you can watch the full interview - with subtitles - above.
But for those that don’t want to watch the full conversation, we’ve picked out some of the key moments from the conversation below.
Enjoy.
PlayStation was not about getting revenge on Nintendo
During the keynote session, Kutaragi talked at length about his history of working with (and eventually against) Nintendo.
“We never think about Sony as a separate entity,” he explains. “We all are a team. With this mentality, I approached the Nintendo headquarters every week by using the bullet train. So, I seemed to be an acting member in Nintendo. “[One woman there] assumed I was their employee. I had a very close relationship [with Nintendo].”
Initially, at around the time of the Famicom, Kutaragi proposed a “very elegant, super fast, and super reliable small, tiny floppy disk”. But Nintendo said it was too late to introduce it.
“They totally gave up with disks at the time. I was a little bit shocked. But they tried to stay in the toy industry. So I understood.”
Kutaragi’s next proposed partnership with Nintendo was around a sound chip for the Super Famicom (or SNES). He asked: “Why is the sound quality of game machines so stupid?” Nintendo had a simple sound solution, and Kutaragi felt they could do better. “Finally, they took our solution. That was a very nice collaboration with the gaming industry.”
It was then that Kutaragi tried to develop a disc system - the PlayStation - for Nintendo.
“Nintendo’s head of R&D almost gave up with removable storage,” Kutaragi said, referring to the period of the original PlayStation’s development. “They stuck with ROM cartridges, [which] are very reliable and very, very fast – [even if you’re ] changing the hardware specification for adding a new chipset within it.
“But if their software partners wanted to repeat their manufacturing volume, because, say, 100,000 units was not enough. People [were] waiting for their game... it took two to three months, because it’s hardware. It seemed to be software, but the reality was it was hardware – [you’re] putting code on the semiconductor and assembling those many parts on the PCB board. The kids could not wait for that whole long period. They’d buy their cartridge from the second-hand market. But that value could not [be returned] back to the software developers. That [wasn’t] healthy for the future.”
Sony wanted to create a disc-based device, but Nintendo had given up on such an idea, and so it told Kutaragi: “Ken, if you want to do it, okay.” This led to the initial PlayStation prototype.
“But some surprises happened,” he laughs. “ At CES, some announcement was circulated that Nintendo was working with another partner. They said CDi would be their next media. But CDi was developed by Sony and Philips jointly. So, I knew their capability. They were using a huge amount of capacity. It took a long, long time for reading the games.
“My idea [was] real-time synthesizing. Those things can be real-time synthesized. Why would they use those old-fashioned media? I have no idea. But I understood, they really wanted to stay in their previous ages.”
“One of my elder team members within Sony started to cry: ‘Sony is not a toy company!’”
It’s often forgotten that the CDi wasn’t just a partnership between Philips and Nintendo, but Sony was involved, too. And Kutaragi faced opposition from inside his own company towards the PlayStation, mainly because of the perception that video games were toys.
“It is a very natural mentality: stay in the old field, we do not want to change anything. Just do those things,” he recalls. “One of my elder team members within Sony started to cry: “Sony is not a toy company!” He [cried]. That was their mentality.”
Ultimately, Kutaragi wanted to change the perception that video games were toys, but could be “a new form of entertainment”. This led to the creation of the first PlayStation. He says it wasn’t, despite how it’s often framed in the media, out of some desire to get revenge on Nintendo.
“Many of the media said, “Sony suffered a betrayal, they will take some revenge.” No. Totally no. We are all friends. Think about it technology-wise, no one had thought that such a real-time computer graphics-based player could happen within the 20th century.”
So has he forgiven Nintendo?
“I love Nintendo,” he insists. “I [contacted them] every week. One of my counterparts there was my best business friend. I love Nintendo games.”
Kutaragi wanted the Xbox to happen
During our conversation, Kutaragi recounted a conversation with Microsoft before it had launched into the console space with Xbox. He even claims partial credit, or at least foresight, for Microsoft’s decision to make a games machine.
“I had the chance to meet with the head of Microsoft one-to-one. He was so arrogant,” he laughed. “I [showed] him what we were developing [for real-time 3D graphics in the home]. He said, ‘Okay, we will send free hard disk drives to Sony, and give some license rights to them.’ He tried to convince me [to take this]. I said only one word: “No” The reason was… I was not so super arrogant [as] they were, [but] I had a dream: if I said no, they would start to bring in another games platform after PC. That was my secret intention. They did, spending huge [amounts of] money on it. After that, we worked together to open up this field. That was very intentional.”
It took Namco just ‘a couple of months’ to get Ridge Racer on PS1
Kutaragi recalled that some companies took a fair amount of convincing to put their games onto discs and that first PlayStation. He even spoke with Sega, who ultimately wanted to stick with their existing strategy (a story that’s been recounted by Sega of America boss Tom Kalinskie).
However, other arcade and coin-op developers were keen to see how their games would perform in the home. Namco and Tamsoft were two such firms, and were delighted to discover how smoothly their titles could be ported to Sony’s first games machine.
“[Namco] took a very short period moving coin-op game Ridge Racer onto PlayStation,” Kutaragi said. “Do you know how long? Just a couple of months! And [Tamsoft’s] first texture-mapped fighting game Toshinden took close to one month [with] under 10 people. Could you believe it?
“We sent them some guidebooks with some sample code, and [worked with] Namco people on checking performance, how many bandwidths or how many calculations [it was] possible [to] squeeze out. We prepared those tools and authoring systems for them. Exciting things were happening.”
Something ‘more elegant’ could replace the game console
Ken Kutaragi believes the age of the console may be coming to an end.
During the Game Republic New Horizons conference, we asked how he sees the future of consoles given the turbulent times the sector is going through. And Kutaragi immediately commented on the rising costs.
“Currently the machines are super expensive.,” he said. “It’s not a healthy situation. You spend huge money on [them, because] graphics boards are super expensive right now.”
He reflected that this is partly due to past decisions made by PlayStation and Xbox to bring their console architecture closer in line with that of PC. The biggest shift for Sony was when the platform holder developed the PlayStation 4, the intention being to make it easier for developers to make games for console and PC simultaneously, thus creating a more integrated market.
“It worked, but right now PC is super expensive– it’s the price of a car, it’s not healthy,” he said.
He noted the connection between these rising prices and the increasing use of AI – something he now has a direct interest in as president and CEO of Cyber AI Entertainment. He added that the technology behind AI is “evolving [into a] much more elegant thing” and this will likely have a direct impact on the video game space.
“The age may be coming where we don’t need any consoles,” he said. “It’s a [real] danger.”
He continued, noting that AI clients will eventually become smaller and more energy efficient, like the human brain..
“Do not think about a huge, super gigantic AI in the future,” he said. “Maybe the brain will be well-distributed, connecting to those clients, those AI systems, and even many other things through some lightweight platform. But it will not be a console, it will not be a smartphone.”
He added, laughing: “This is not the official comment from Sony Interactive Entertainment!”
Ultimately, he’s highly optimistic on how AI could transform entertainment.
“Everything can be calculatable. The AI is elaborating, but it’s at an intermediate stage. Maybe in the future, everything [will] be calculatable. Everything,” he says.
“If those things happen, what entertainment could we and our children create for the future? Those things will not take several decades. Maybe it will be coming very, very soon. Be prepared for that.”
Stay curious, don’t get stuck in the past
We ended our conversation by asking Kutaragi for his advice for the next generation of game makers and engineers.
“Keep chasing your dream,” he says simply. “Curiosity is very important. And collaboration is also very exciting. And do not spend huge money and time just sticking on previous things. That’s my advice.”
